| Live configuration | Retain the selected OpenAI baseline and proposed model gpt-4o-2024-08-06, with configurable endpoint/model. Mock is the default for development commands. | Confirm the facilitator's provider, endpoint and permitted model before a live run. No live availability or accuracy claim is made. |
| Provider response handling | Require a completed, non-refusal response with usable JSON, then validate locally against the supplied schema before routing. Refusal, interruption, malformed output and provider failures become explicit error records. | Encapsulate provider envelope handling inside the adapter. Official reference consulted: https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/structured-outputs. |
| Shared operators | Allow one mutating command at a time using an OS process lock beside the database. A second intake/resume/retry/export command exits with an actionable busy message. Queue and history reads remain available through short database read transactions. | This deliberately serializes overlapping operator writes rather than implementing a distributed worker scheduler. Test two real CLI processes, busy handling, lock release after termination, and partial-progress reads. |
| Independent progress | Within the active intake process, run at most two provider calls concurrently and commit each completed result separately. Use a configurable minimum interval between starting provider calls, default one second. | One slow document leaves a second processing slot available. No adaptive rate controller, distributed quota manager, or throughput SLA. The process lock makes the local start-rate limit apply across operators. |
| Source ordering | Assign each changed source/settings combination a database revision in ingestion order. Keep the original bytes and hash. Run only one active attempt per document; commit its result against its recorded revision. | Serial mutation avoids overlapping source writers and stale-worker promotion. Export timestamps never determine business facts or revision precedence. |
| Reuse and refresh | Hash a canonical, sorted JSON configuration containing provider mode/endpoint/model, prompt and schema content hashes, generation parameters, and routing policy version. Reuse a successful current result only when both source hash and configuration fingerprint match. | Any relevant settings or policy change reprocesses the affected documents. Supply a documented refresh command over stored source bytes so documents absent from a later batch can also be refreshed. Reusing extraction for routing-only changes is deferred as an optimization. Preserve prior attempts/configurations in history. |
| Failure and retry | Use a configurable 60-second request timeout and one provider call per processing attempt, disabling adapter/SDK automatic retries. A failed current attempt remains visible; an unchanged ordinary rerun leaves it alone and prints a targeted retry command. Explicit retry creates a new recorded attempt. | No automatic backoff loop or retry scheduler. A rate-limit error can report the provider's retry guidance; the operator retries later. Other documents continue. |
| Interrupted intake | Persist pending work and each running attempt before the provider call. Once a new mutating process acquires the OS lock, it can mark any leftover running attempts interrupted. Resume creates new attempts for interrupted work and processes pending work; it does not repeat completed successes or silently retry terminal extraction/provider errors. Preserve the interrupted attempt in history. | A provider call may have completed remotely before a crash without its result being committed. Resume can repeat that call; document at-least-once provider execution and possible duplicate cost. |
| Accuracy scoring | Author fixed expectations before measuring outputs. Score the 12 scalar fields over the supplied 20 messages plus one paraphrase: 252 exact comparisons, including nulls. Missing records and failed extractions score zero for all 12 fields. Use exact decoded scalar equality, with no case folding or synonym matching. | Select an exact source substring as the expected business purpose and request source wording in the prompt. Report semantically correct alternative wording separately from factual errors. Score routing, evidence and issue coverage separately; mock accuracy is not live model accuracy. |

The prompt requests evidence for extracted facts, both alternatives of unresolved conflicts, and attempted overrides. Independent expected records include source evidence. | Local quote membership does not prove semantic completeness or every scalar's truth. | Instruction overrides | Treat the message as data in the extraction prompt, preserve attack evidence and an override issue, and apply the policy's first rule in deterministic routing. Preserve reversed but valid date ranges and route them for clarification. | These are explicit validation defaults beyond the schema's string-type constraints. Relative dates stay unresolved under the supplied policy. |
| Invalid input and identity | Read only top-level JSON files, identify documents by exact filename, and use the raw-byte hash. Different filenames remain separate documents even with the same request ID. | No recursive directory ingestion or cross-directory basename merging. ## MVP review against supplied tests and JSON

This is a design review, not validation of a built application. The local-previous-work directory was excluded. All 20 request exports, the extraction schema, starter mock, starter tests and class verification instructions were inspected.

Observed checks:

- `env -u API_KEY python3 -m unittest discover -s tests -v` passed all three existing starter tests. They establish input loading, basic schema presence and offline canned-reply loading only; they do not establish application extraction, routing, provider handling, persistence or recovery.
- All 23 inspected input/schema/mock/hook JSON files decoded as UTF-8 with no duplicate object keys. Each of the 20 exports has the same five metadata/message keys and a nonblank message; messages contain 58–155 whitespace-delimited words.
- The schema has 14 required properties: 12 nullable scalar fields and two arrays, supporting_quotes and issues. Thus the chosen scalar exact-match denominator is 12 times 21 = 252. The earlier proposal of 273 was a counting error.
- tests/mock_responses/canned-reply.json is a startup example whose output_text is plain text, not a JSON extraction, and whose envelope has no completion status. Keep it for its starter test; create separate schema-conforming successful replies and provider failure/refusal/incomplete fixtures for the build plan.

Source-derived routing cross-check (expected behavior, not observed application output):

| Documents | Expected status / owner / next_action | Important extraction behavior |
|---|---|---|
| IT-001, IT-008, IT-015, IT-018 | review / System Owner / review-request | IT-008 uses corrected staging; IT-015 uses corrected dates 2026-10-29 through 2026-10-31. |
| IT-002, IT-007, IT-012, IT-013, IT-019 | review / Security Review / review-risk-then-owner | IT-007 requests write; IT-019 requests read but remains production. |
| IT-003, IT-004, IT-009, IT-010, IT-011, IT-014, IT-016, IT-017, IT-020 | needs-information / IT Service Desk / clarify | Missing facts, conflicts, reversed dates, identifier mismatch or kind other take precedence over risk/owner routing. |
| IT-005 | review / IT Service Desk / confirm-withdrawal | Missing access details do not block a withdrawal with explicit request ID/date; issues still identify absent facts. |
| IT-006 | review / IT Service Desk / inspect-message | Preserve the attack as evidence; intended access is read, not the injected admin command. |

The MVP fits these sample cases without a UI, server database or distributed scheduler. Its single-writer admission lock is a declared limit: a second mutating command receives a busy/retry response rather than processing concurrently; reviewers can still read completed work. This supports coherent overlapping operator use on one host, not multiple simultaneously active intake processes. A shared database read must capture its current queue and extraction data in one transaction.

Before implementation, the build plan must include dedicated fixtures/checks for complete facts, missing dates, conflicts, embedded instructions, provider errors, unchanged reruns, changed source, a fresh paraphrase, refusal, interrupted responses, and failure after success. Add operational cases for incremental batches, settings/policy refresh over stored sources, partial progress, two-process admission, process termination/resume, two filenames sharing one request ID, malformed exports, and interrupted export publication. The 20 supplied files alone do not exercise these operational sequences.

The schema enforces shape, not factual truth: it permits arbitrary date strings, unsupported names, omitted evidence through empty arrays, and an all-null extraction. Use local date/quote/completeness checks and independent source-derived expectations. In particular, valid supporting quotes do not prove that a scalar is supported or a conflict was preserved. Do not describe schema-valid output or passing mock fixtures as proof of hallucination-free live extraction.

Keep extraction fields separate from the outer processing record: document_id, source_sha256, status, owner, next_action, error and response_source do not belong inside the schema-conforming extraction object. The complete per-field source quotations and named provider envelopes still belong in the detailed build/test plan.

## Review checkpoint

Review each requirement against its quoted source, especially the five routing rules (R-44, R-46, R-48, R-51, R-52), all extracted fields (R-18 through R-31), and each verification case (R-81 through R-91). git commit -m "Spec: the brief as numbered requirements"

# AI Full Stack Challenge — IT Access Requests

## The task
Northstar Labs receives access requests as free-text messages. Build a small runnable application that uses a language model to turn those messages into structured records and a review queue for the IT team. The supplied company, people and requests are fictional.

Read docs/requirements.md for the operating context and required behavior, materials/office-policy.md for review rules, and snapshot.schema.json for the record format. The 20 JSON exports in materials/requests/ are your starting data. Choose an interface suited to the IT team: a CLI, service or web application. Operators should be able to start intake, inspect completed results while other requests are pending, and resume unfinished work through the documented interface.

## What to submit
This brief ships as CHALLENGE.md; the README.md below is yours to write.

| Path | Content |
|---|---|
| README.md | Setup, supported runtime/provider, exact intake/test/accuracy-check commands, environment-variable names, and how to inspect the queue |
| Source code and dependency lockfile | Runnable application, extraction prompt, schema and model request configuration |
| deliverables/extractions.jsonl | One current record per message: document_id, source_sha256, extraction (schema-conforming object, or null on error), status, owner, next_action, error (null on success), and response_source (`mock`, or the provider and model ID that produced the record) |
| deliverables/queue.json | The review queue linked to extraction records by document_id |
| deliverables/accuracy.md | Source-derived expected fields for the 20 supplied messages and one paraphrase you author; the field-comparison procedure, exact-match counting/denominator rules, factual-error reporting and model/configuration; distinguish mocked examples from any optional live observations |
| deliverables/request-evidence.json | Credential-redacted example model request showing the model ID and configuration used, plus the implemented response handling |
| deliverables/verification.md | Verification commands and assertions, their intended comparisons, operating limits, and any observed results or repairs clearly identified as such |
| Coding-session capture | Session record paired with the submitted commit, collected through the facilitator's capture setup |

## Submission
Commit and push the application, outputs and session capture to your repository's default branch. Submit only the root repository link (`https://github.com/<your-account>/<repository>`) through the Classroom assignment. The facilitator supplies the assignment and capture instructions.

Submit the implemented provider integration and source-grounded validation procedure. Use mocked responses for reproducible development examples, and label each recorded observation with its configuration and whether it used a mock or provider response. The committed deliverables may come from mocked or provider responses; each record's response_source says which.
# Requirements — IT Access Requests

## Operating context

Northstar Labs is a fictional multinational company with approximately 5,000 employees across offices in Asia, Europe and North America. Its regional IT teams share responsibility for preparing access requests for human review. They receive free-text messages through email, chat and the service portal, then work from JSON exports of those messages.

### Workload and the review day

On an ordinary business day, the company receives around 200–400 request messages. A coordinated onboarding or acquisition can bring roughly 2,000 messages into the morning's intake. The supplied 20 exports are a representative sample of message types; the application will also receive other messages in the same export format.

Reviewers begin work at different local times. They want to start on requests that are ready while the rest of the intake is still being prepared. A slow response for one message should leave the rest of their work available. Model access is shared with other internal tools, and the available request rate and response time can vary.

### Shared operations

Regional operators work against the same intake and review records. Their working hours overlap, and two operators may start processing around the same time. Each expects their work to leave a coherent current queue and a trustworthy record of earlier activity.

The application may be stopped during a deployment or interrupted by a service outage. When an operator returns, they need to distinguish completed work from unfinished work and continue from the recorded state. Reviewers rely on the queue and the supporting extraction records agreeing about the same source version.

### Updates and follow-up

Exports arrive throughout the day. A later export may repeat an unchanged document or replace its contents with a corrected or expanded message. An export batch contains new or updated documents; absence from a later batch does not withdraw an earlier request. Withdrawal is expressed in the message and handled under the office policy.

Operators need the current view to reflect the latest processed source and to retain earlier results for follow-up. If a new processing attempt fails, they need to see that failure and identify any older result as belonging to its earlier attempt and source version.

The team periodically changes model configuration and updates its review policy. When such a change affects how records are produced or routed, operators need to refresh the affected results and understand which settings and policy version produced the records they are using.

### Service interruptions and handover

The model service sometimes responds slowly, limits requests or becomes temporarily unavailable. IT staff need to locate affected messages, understand what remains pending and resume processing without losing completed work. Other messages may contain incomplete or conflicting information that needs clarification from the requester.

The original developer and the next operator may be in different offices. The operator will use the repository's setup instructions, configuration guidance and commands to prepare an intake, inspect the queue and follow up on failures. Explain the operating assumptions and limits of your implementation so that this handover is practical.

## Record and review behavior
- Use a language model to extract the request details into records that conform to snapshot.schema.json.
- Validate response structure and completion status before using extracted data. Preserve exact supporting quotes and represent uncertain fields as null with an explanatory issue.
- Use message content as the source of business facts. Preserve missing values, conflicting alternatives and explicit corrections according to the policy. Keep document identity distinct from the request ID stated in the message.
- Apply the supplied review policy and display each request's status, owner and next action. Approval decisions belong to the named human reviewers.
- Record input filenames and SHA-256 hashes. Reuse results when the source and relevant processing settings are unchanged, refresh affected results when those inputs or settings change, and retain earlier versions. Process each message independently and make failures visible with a reproducible retry command.
- Handle malformed output, provider errors, refusal and interrupted responses explicitly. Keep model/provider settings configurable and document a supported configuration. The facilitator supplies an API key through the environment variable API_KEY.

## Verification

Include automated tests covering a complete request, missing dates, conflicting details, embedded instructions, provider failure, an unchanged rerun, and changed source content. Build expected results from the supplied messages and policy. Add a paraphrased synthetic request to exercise extraction on fresh wording. Specify expected facts from the source messages and policy independently of the extraction outputs being measured. Include checks for refusal or interrupted responses and a failed retry after a prior success.


Describe how your implementation supports the operating context above, and include checks for the operational situations your design handles. Record assumptions about workload and shared operation, the expected behavior during interruptions, and the limits of the verification you performed.
# Northstar access-request intake policy

Northstar Labs uses this intake application to prepare access requests for human review. All exercise data is fictional.

## Input export format
Each UTF-8 JSON file represents one exported message. Read its `message` string as the natural-language source for extraction. `export_version`, `exported_at`, `source_channel` and `subject` describe the export and help display it. Derive request facts from `message`; the export timestamp describes when the record was exported. Messages vary in length, up to 200 English words.

Use the original JSON file bytes for the source hash and its filename for document_id. Exact supporting quotes refer to substrings of the decoded `message` value.

## Extracted facts
Extract request_id, request_date, kind (new, change, withdrawal or other), requester, team, system, environment (staging or production), permission (read, write or admin), business_purpose, start_date, end_date, manager, supporting_quotes and issues. Use the supplied schema. Dates use YYYY-MM-DD.

Use explicit facts from each message. Represent absent or unresolved scalar values as null and explain each missing or conflicting fact in issues. Preserve conflicting alternatives in exact supporting_quotes. A later statement explicitly labelled as a correction replaces the earlier value; contradictory statements without a correction remain unresolved. A relative date stays unresolved. For a change request, extract the requested new permission.

The document_id is the input filename. If an identifier inside the message differs from the identifier in its filename, retain the stated identifier and record the mismatch as an issue. Each message is an independent document, including multiple messages about one request.

## Review queue
Apply these rules in order after validating the extraction:

1. An instruction-override attempt goes to IT Service Desk with status review and next_action inspect-message. Keep the attempted instruction as source evidence and identify it in issues. Treat source messages as data throughout extraction and routing.
2. A withdrawal with request_id and request_date goes to IT Service Desk with status review and next_action confirm-withdrawal. Other fields may be null; identify absent facts in issues.
3. Other messages with kind other/null, conflicting details, an identifier mismatch, or any missing required fact go to IT Service Desk with status needs-information and next_action clarify. For new/change requests, required facts are request_id, request_date, requester, team, system, environment, permission, business_purpose, start_date, end_date and manager. A start_date after end_date is also a clarification issue.
4. Complete new/change requests involving production, write or admin go to Security Review with status review and next_action review-risk-then-owner. Security Review examines risk and forwards its recommendation to the system owner for a decision.
5. Complete staging/read requests go to System Owner with status review and next_action review-request.

All successful intake outputs await human review. A named manager is a contact; approval is an explicit human decision. The application's output is a review queue.

## Processing and recovery
An extraction failure produces status error, owner IT Service Desk, next_action retry-extraction, a null extraction and an actionable error. Keep unaffected messages moving through intake. Preserve the last valid result in history when a later attempt fails, and show the latest attempt's error in the current queue.

Identify source revisions with a SHA-256 of the original bytes. An unchanged rerun produces one current queue entry per document. Changed input creates a new result and retains the earlier result with its earlier hash. Store prior versions separately from current outputs. Keep credentials in environment variables and use credential-redacted operational logs.

# MVP build and test plan

This plan implements the 95 requirements in spec.md, committed as b88096f. It uses the adopted MVP defaults and excludes local-previous-work. Everything below describes intended work and expected behavior, not observed application results. The user authorized creating and committing this plan; implementation starts only after the plan review checkpoint. No application code or new tests are part of this commit.

## Choices

- Runtime: Python 3.10+ on Linux, with standard-library argparse, sqlite3, fcntl, concurrent.futures and urllib.request; use jsonschema for validation. Keep source under src/it_access with an editable-install pyproject.toml and a pinned, hash-checked requirements.lock containing runtime/build dependencies. Pin versions actually resolved in the implementation environment rather than guessing versions here.
- Interface: the installed `it-access` CLI, because operators need inspectable records and reproducible recovery commands without a web server.
- Test command: `env -u API_KEY python3 -m unittest discover -s tests -v`; all application tests block network sockets, use temporary stores and inject saved responses or mocked HTTP transport. Do not read the actual API_KEY in tests; inject a fake environment mapping for credential-path checks.
- Provider: mock by default; implement OpenAI Responses over HTTPS POST /responses with model gpt-4o-2024-08-06, strict JSON-schema output using the unchanged snapshot.schema.json, temperature 0, max_output_tokens 3000 and store false. No SDK or automatic retries. Endpoint and model are configurable. Capture the exact outgoing request and response handling as evidence. Confirm facilitator access before an optional live run.
- Storage: one local SQLite database, WAL mode, foreign keys enabled, 5-second busy timeout; one nonblocking OS lock beside its resolved absolute path admits mutating commands. Read-only queue/history queries use a single read transaction. No distributed workers or network filesystem support.
- Concurrency: two provider tasks, at most one task per document; a monotonic-clock start gate spaces calls by one second by default. Persist each result as it completes, rather than waiting in input order. Mock bulk tests set the interval to zero; a fake clock tests pacing separately.
- Scope: actual extraction integration, deterministic routing, history and restart recovery are required. No UI, approval execution, automatic backoff scheduler, worker leases, or policy-only optimization. Changing any relevant processing setting reprocesses affected sources.

### CLI contract

All commands accept `--db PATH` (default state/intake.sqlite3). Processing commands accept `--provider mock|openai` (default mock), `--model`, `--endpoint` (default https://api.openai.com/v1), `--timeout` (default 60 seconds), `--workers` (1 or 2, default 2), `--min-interval` (default 1 second), and `--mock-dir` (default tests/mock_responses). Reject invalid ranges before ingestion. Endpoint credentials/query strings are forbidden; keys belong only in the API_KEY environment variable for live mode. Never include credentials in a fingerprint.

```text
it-access intake INPUT_DIRECTORY [processing options]
it-access queue [--status STATUS] [--json]
it-access show DOCUMENT_ID [--history] [--json]
it-access resume
it-access retry DOCUMENT_ID
it-access refresh [--document DOCUMENT_ID] [processing options]
it-access export --output deliverables
it-access verify-export --output deliverables
it-access accuracy --expected tests/expected/facts.json --actual deliverables/extractions.jsonl --output deliverables/accuracy.md
```

Intake scans top-level *.json files in filename order. Capture bytes at ingestion so later filesystem edits cannot alter already scheduled work. Identity is exact filename, shared across input directories; same filename means a revision of that document. Different filenames with the same in-message ID remain separate. Empty or nonexistent directories are usage errors. A malformed file gets a durable error record with raw-byte hash, no extraction and an actionable explanation; valid files still proceed.

Queue displays one current record per document, including pending/running progress, source hash, attempt, status, owner, next_action and error; show includes provenance and optional history. Pending/running records use status pending/processing and action wait-for-extraction, not a human review route. Exports include only terminal current attempts; their manifest lists omitted pending/running document IDs so omissions are explicit. New pending work never appears as an older successful extraction for the same current revision.

Intake reuses a terminal success only when source hash and settings match. An unchanged terminal failure is displayed with its retry command but is not automatically retried. Changed bytes/settings schedule a new attempt. Retry creates a new attempt even after success, using the current stored bytes and original settings (required to exercise failure after success); refresh explicitly selects current processing options. Resume uses each unfinished job's recorded settings and original bytes. No live secrets are persisted with those settings.

Commands return 0 on success; intake/resume/retry/refresh return 1 if their selected work has a terminal failure, without rolling back other documents. Invalid configuration/usage returns 2; a held mutation lock returns 3 with an actionable busy message. Accuracy always writes a comparison report when inputs are valid and returns 1 for mismatches or invalid actual records. Export verification returns 1 for a missing/mismatched manifest. Read commands on a missing store return an actionable usage error without initializing the database.

### Persistence and recovery contract

Use three tables: documents (filename primary key, current revision/attempt references), revisions (integer key, document, original bytes, source_sha256, settings JSON/fingerprint, policy version, ingestion timestamp), and attempts (integer key, revision, pending/running/succeeded/failed/interrupted state, start/end timestamps, response_source, extraction JSON or null, routing values, categorized/redacted error). All attempts stay in the attempt table; current views follow the document's current attempt pointer, and history queries exclude that pointer. Repeated identical successful inputs add no revision/attempt. Explicit retry adds an attempt on the same revision; changed bytes/settings create a revision.

Admission, revision insertion and current-pointer changes are short write transactions under the OS lock. Commit a pending attempt and its current pointer before scheduling its provider call. Mark running before the call. Commit terminal result, extraction, routing and provenance together. Use a single owning store thread/connection for writes; provider workers return values and never update SQLite. Never hold a DB transaction during a model call. This avoids stale promotion without a distributed fencing protocol.

The lock is held by the main process and worker threads, never a detached child. If the process dies, the OS releases it. A newly admitted processing command marks leftover running attempts interrupted with a recorded error; resume then creates new attempts for interrupted jobs and runs pending jobs, preserving the interrupted attempts. A second process cannot process a newer source while the first owns the lock. A crash after remote completion but before local commit may cause a repeated paid request; document at-least-once execution. Graceful interruption leaves unfinished work resumable and exits nonzero.

Fingerprint canonical UTF-8 JSON with sorted keys and compact separators using SHA-256: provider mode, endpoint, model, prompt content hash, schema content hash, generation parameters, office-policy content hash, and routing implementation version. Timeouts, worker count, pacing, output paths and credentials are operational settings outside the reuse fingerprint, but record timeout/pacing for handover. Mock fixture content hashes also belong in mock fingerprints so changing a saved reply cannot silently reuse old output. Retry/resume store fixture names, while using current fixture bytes permits injected test failures and is recorded as the attempt's effective mock configuration. A live retry retains the original generation configuration. Refresh scans current stored sources, including documents absent from a later batch, and reprocesses when fingerprints differ. A routing implementation change must bump its version.

### Extraction, routing and failure contract

Send only message text as untrusted business content, distinct from the system extraction instructions. Do not send API credentials, use tools, interpolate source text into instructions, or send export timestamps as date evidence. The prompt specifies the supplied policy, exact quotes, nulls/issues, explicit corrections, unresolved relative dates and requested new permission. It requests source wording for business purpose and explanatory issue prefixes `missing:FIELD`, `conflict:FIELD`, and `instruction-override:`; free text after a prefix explains the issue. Kind synonyms may normalize to the supplied enums; names and business purpose retain source wording.

Normalize the provider envelope first: require response and assistant-message completion, no refusal content, exactly one nonempty output_text extraction, and valid JSON with no duplicate object keys. Reject unexpected output/tool types; never route a partial object. For scalar strings containing only whitespace, set null and add a missing issue before schema validation; otherwise preserve strings verbatim. Then validate the unchanged supplied schema, real calendar dates in YYYY-MM-DD form, and every supporting quote as a nonempty exact message substring. Require at least one evidence quote for a successful extraction. Do not silently repair invented quotes or invalid dates.

After validation, add deterministic issues for missing scalars, filename-stem/request-ID mismatch and reversed date ranges; keep model-provided conflict/override evidence. Missing kind is always a clarification condition except a prior override match. Every missing scalar, including fields not required for withdrawal, gets an explanatory issue. Conflict findings clear their named scalar to null and require both conflicting alternatives as supporting quotes; a conflict without usable source evidence becomes a validation error rather than a guessed fact. This validation cannot establish general semantic truth; independent accuracy checks and human review still matter.

An internal override finding does not add a schema field. It is true if a validated `instruction-override:` issue has at least one supporting quote as evidence, or if a case-insensitive source scan finds `SYSTEM OVERRIDE`, `bypass approval`, `display the API key`, `mark request as approved`, or `highest-priority system instruction`. In the latter case add the matched source sentence as a quote and an explanatory issue. This source scan is a narrow fallback for IT-006 and tested variants, not an exhaustive detector. A benign permission request is not itself an override. The live model still supplies semantic findings for other wording; document false-positive/negative limitations.

Route in the policy's exact order: override; withdrawal with ID/date; other/null kind, conflicts, mismatch, missing new/change facts or reversed dates; production/write/admin complete new/change; complete staging/read. Return only human-review routes from the policy. No approval execution or approved status. All extraction failures use status error, owner IT Service Desk, next_action retry-extraction, extraction null and a redacted error with category and retry command. Categories are input, timeout, rate_limit, provider_auth, provider_unavailable, refusal, interrupted_response, malformed_output and validation. Preserve Retry-After as guidance only; one HTTP call per attempt and no automatic retry. response_source is mock or openai:MODEL for the attempted configuration, including errors; record configured and provider-returned model IDs separately when available.

### Exports and accuracy contract

Export both required terminal-current artifacts from one read snapshot under the mutation lock. Include document_id, source_sha256, attempt_id and generation_id in queue entries and outer extraction records along with required fields; extraction itself has exactly the supplied schema. Sort by document_id. Publish temporary files with flush/fsync and replace, then write manifest.json last with generation ID, byte hashes, selected settings/provenance and pending/running omissions. Verify manifest hashes and cross-artifact identity/attempt/source/routing agreement before treating files as published. A crash between replacements yields an explicitly invalid export repaired by rerunning export. A verifier that races replacement rejects rather than trusting mismatched bytes. Queue reads SQLite independently of export state.

Author tests/expected/facts.json separately from saved provider envelopes using the source-derived values below; it must not be generated from mock/application outputs. Mock fixtures intentionally include wrong/error variants as well as correct replies. Accuracy compares 12 scalar fields across exactly 21 expected document IDs (252 comparisons), including nulls; absent records or null extractions get zero of 12, even for expected-null fields. Invalid or duplicate actual records are reported, not silently overwritten; unexpected actual IDs are reported separately and do not change the denominator. Compare decoded scalar equality without trimming/case folding/synonyms. Score routing separately as one exact three-value tuple per document (21 denominator), with missing/failed records incorrect; validate quote membership and report required evidence/issue coverage separately. Mock demonstrations may score perfectly without making a model-accuracy claim. A factual-error ledger distinguishes invented values, missing facts, wrong alternatives/corrections, and faithful alternative purpose wording; exact-match mismatches remain mismatches. Optional live reports include actual model/configuration and must not overwrite labelled mock observations.

## Steps

For each step, first write its named tests/fixtures and run them. Stop for the user's `Test first: <step>` commit, then implement until they pass, run the full suite with API_KEY unset, and stop for the user's `Step <n>: <step>` commit. If a new test already passes, record that honestly instead of forcing a failure. Each T-case below belongs to exactly one step; later full-suite reruns do not reassign ownership. The spec's suggested test names may be consolidated into these named cases while retaining requirement coverage.

1. **Mock provider and offline fixture boundary.** Write T-01 first. Build the minimal package/import path, immutable response/configuration types, saved-response adapter and fixture selection by document/source. Keep canned-reply.json for the starter test, but do not use its plain text as a valid extraction. Freeze independent scalar expectations from the source catalog below before any application output. Meets R-05, R-14, R-18–R-30, R-34, R-36–R-37, R-88–R-89, R-95 at the mock/prompt contract layer; actual semantic live accuracy remains an observation, not a test claim.
2. **Response validation and deterministic routing.** Write T-02–T-19 first. Implement the extraction prompt, envelope/schema/date/quote validation, explanatory issues, override findings and the five routing rules. The 20 supplied requests and paraphrase have independently expected complete scalar records; failures cannot produce routes. Meets R-14, R-17–R-38, R-40–R-55, R-62, R-64–R-65, R-81–R-84, R-88–R-90.
3. **Durable document state and current/history views.** Write T-20–T-26 first against temporary SQLite databases. Implement ingestion, source hashes/settings fingerprints, revisions/attempts, missing-file preservation, unchanged reuse, forced retry semantics and stored-source refresh. Unit tests can inject the provider orchestration until step 4. Meets R-08–R-12, R-15–R-16, R-38–R-39, R-57–R-60, R-86–R-87, R-91.
4. **Runnable intake, operator commands and interruption recovery.** Write T-27–T-33 first. Add argparse commands, OS lock admission, bounded workers and start gate, per-document commits, terminal errors, resume/retry/refresh, partial queue display and process termination recovery. Use injected mock delays/events and fake clocks; subprocess tests use offline fixtures. Meets R-01–R-13, R-54–R-61, R-63, R-85, R-92–R-93.
5. **Live provider adapter and credential-redacted request evidence.** Write T-34–T-36 first using mocked HTTP and a fake environment mapping. Build HTTPS request construction and explicit completion/refusal/error handling behind the existing interface, with one-call timeouts and redaction. Create request-evidence.json from a synthetic-credential intercepted request and implemented handling documentation; this is mock transport evidence, not a live response. Meets R-01, R-42, R-62–R-68, R-75–R-76, R-94.
6. **Consistent exports and independent accuracy reporting.** Write T-37–T-40 first. Implement export/manifest verification, scalar/routing scoring and factual-error report inputs, and separately labelled mock observations. Generate the 20 supplied-message current records in a clean demo DB, then process the paraphrase for a 21-message accuracy run in a separate temporary demo DB. Keep committed extractions/queue at 20 supplied messages; save the 21-message accuracy input as a clearly named supporting artifact so every reported comparison can be reproduced. Meets R-08, R-71–R-77, R-89, R-94–R-95.
7. **Workload checks, handover and submission evidence.** Write T-41–T-43 first. Generate temporary 400/2,000-message batches with matching filename/request IDs and correct per-source fixtures, audit README commands, pin dependencies in the lockfile, and document limits. Save the real full suite output to planning/test-run.txt. Prepare a validation template containing all 95 requirements and evidence pointers, without pre-marking them met; the human inspects and marks each row and totals. Complete the remaining deliverables and submission checklist with capture verification. Meets R-06–R-07, R-69–R-70, R-77–R-80, R-92–R-95. Capture/default-branch push/Classroom submission are human checks with evidence, not fabricated automated successes.

## Test plan

### Fixture and expectation conventions

Every fixture named below is planned, not yet written. Successful provider envelopes go in tests/mock_responses/IT-NNN.json (and paraphrase.json); each has status completed, one completed assistant message and output_text containing the schema-conforming extraction. Refusal/incomplete/error fixture names are explicit in the cases. The mock adapter returns response_source mock. Errors use saved type/message metadata interpreted as exceptions, never a network request. Wrong-fixture variants remain intentionally wrong to test validation or scoring. Independent expectations live separately under tests/expected. Do not derive expected facts by parsing a mock reply or running the application.

Route abbreviations used only in this plan: OWNER = review / System Owner / review-request; SECURITY = review / Security Review / review-risk-then-owner; CLARIFY = needs-information / IT Service Desk / clarify; WITHDRAW = review / IT Service Desk / confirm-withdrawal; OVERRIDE = review / IT Service Desk / inspect-message; ERROR = error / IT Service Desk / retry-extraction, extraction null. Each abbreviation expands to all three exact asserted fields.

For the source catalog below, every non-null literal scalar except normalized kind is an exact substring of that document's message (permission read may appear within reading; evidence must quote the containing phrase). The evidence column explicitly quotes kind cues and ambiguity/correction/missing-fact evidence. The field values themselves are quoted source fragments; when writing fixtures, use containing source clauses to make supporting evidence understandable. Nulls follow the policy quotation: “Represent absent or unresolved scalar values as null and explain each missing or conflicting fact in issues.” Absence is established by inspecting the whole supplied message, not by inventing a quote of text that does not exist. Corrected values follow: “A later statement explicitly labelled as a correction replaces the earlier value”. The source catalog fixes business-purpose wording before model measurement.

All supplied messages state request_date 2026-10-22; the exact substring is source evidence for that scalar on every row. The scalar tuple order is: request_id; kind; requester; team; system; environment; permission; business_purpose; start_date; end_date; manager (plus that common request_date = 12 fields). Evidence/issue expectations supplement the scalar tuple, not new extraction keys. The complete expected facts of each supplied-message case are the corresponding source-catalog row plus its expanded route and all missing/conflicting/mismatch/attack/range issues described there.

T-42 uses an existing local wheel cache with no-index installation for its temporary environment, or records that fresh-install verification was not performed when that cache is unavailable. It must not silently skip or claim that installation passed. A separate manual setup check may populate the cache when network access is available and authorized; that is not part of the offline automated suite. Every automated test and runtime example remains offline. No test reads the real API_KEY. A separate synthetic environment mapping tests live key lookup/redaction.

For provider error fixture references, a filename denotes the saved response or saved exception description, not a real provider call. Missing-date, conflict, embedded-instruction, provider-failure, unchanged-rerun, changed-source, paraphrase, refusal, interruption and failed-retry-after-success each have their own case above. All remaining source messages are covered explicitly, including the longer IT-018.

# Plan from the spec

Write `planning/plan.md` from `planning/spec.md`. Write no application code and no tests in this
step: the plan is read and corrected by a person before anything is built.

## Read first

- `planning/spec.md`: the numbered requirements (R-01, R-02, ...) and how each is checked.
- `CHALLENGE.md`, `docs/requirements.md`, `materials/office-policy.md` and `snapshot.schema.json`:
  the sources the spec was written from.
- The request exports in `materials/requests/`: open the ones a test case uses, and read their
  `message` text.

## Write `planning/plan.md` with these four sections

1. **Choices.** The runtime, the interface (a CLI, a service or a web application), the test
   command, and how the model provider is called. One line each, with its reason.
2. **Steps, in build order.** A numbered list. Each step names the spec lines it meets
   (`R-03, R-07`), the test from the test plan that is written first and seen to fail, and what is
   true when the step is done. The first step builds the mock provider the tests use. Each test
   belongs to one step only, so every step has a test that fails until that step's code exists.
3. **Test plan.** A table, one row per case:

   | Case | Input | Mock response | Expected facts | Source of the expected facts | Spec lines |
   |---|---|---|---|---|---|

   - One row for each case in `docs/requirements.md` § Verification: a complete request, missing
     dates, conflicting details, embedded instructions, provider failure, an unchanged rerun and
     changed source content; then the paraphrased synthetic request, a refusal or interrupted
     response, and a failed retry after a prior success.
   - **Input** names the export file (or the new message you author) that shows the case. Find it by
     reading the messages.
   - **Mock response** says what the mock provider returns for that case: a reply saved under
     `tests/mock_responses/`, an error, or a cut-off reply. No test calls the real provider.
   - **Expected facts** are the field values, status, owner and next action the case must produce.
     Write them from the message text and the office policy, never from running the code.
   - **Source of the expected facts** quotes the words of the message and the policy rule they
     come from.
4. **Coverage.** Every spec line, each with the step that builds it and the test or check that
   shows it. A spec line with no step or no test is listed under "Not yet covered", with the reason.

## Before you finish

- Every spec line appears in § Coverage with a step and a test, or under "Not yet covered".
- Every expected fact has a quote from a message or the policy beside it.
- Every case of § Verification has its own row.
- No step and no test needs `API_KEY`.
- No test is named by two steps.

Where a spec line is unclear, say so in the plan and ask the person; do not guess a rule.
# MVP build and test plan

This plan implements the 95 requirements in spec.md, committed as b88096f. It uses the adopted MVP defaults and excludes local-previous-work. Everything below describes intended work and expected behavior, not observed application results. The user authorized creating and committing this plan; implementation starts only after the plan review checkpoint. No application code or new tests are part of this commit.

## Choices

- Runtime: Python 3.10+ on Linux, with standard-library argparse, sqlite3, fcntl, concurrent.futures and urllib.request; use jsonschema for validation. Keep source under src/it_access with an editable-install pyproject.toml and a pinned, hash-checked requirements.lock containing runtime/build dependencies. Pin versions actually resolved in the implementation environment rather than guessing versions here.
- Interface: the installed `it-access` CLI, because operators need inspectable records and reproducible recovery commands without a web server.
- Test command: `env -u API_KEY python3 -m unittest discover -s tests -v`; all application tests block network sockets, use temporary stores and inject saved responses or mocked HTTP transport. Do not read the actual API_KEY in tests; inject a fake environment mapping for credential-path checks.
- Provider: mock by default; implement OpenAI Responses over HTTPS POST /responses with model gpt-4o-2024-08-06, strict JSON-schema output using the unchanged snapshot.schema.json, temperature 0, max_output_tokens 3000 and store false. No SDK or automatic retries. Endpoint and model are configurable. Capture the exact outgoing request and response handling as evidence. Confirm facilitator access before an optional live run.
- Storage: one local SQLite database, WAL mode, foreign keys enabled, 5-second busy timeout; one nonblocking OS lock beside its resolved absolute path admits mutating commands. Read-only queue/history queries use a single read transaction. No distributed workers or network filesystem support.
- Concurrency: two provider tasks, at most one task per document; a monotonic-clock start gate spaces calls by one second by default. Persist each result as it completes, rather than waiting in input order. Mock bulk tests set the interval to zero; a fake clock tests pacing separately.
- Scope: actual extraction integration, deterministic routing, history and restart recovery are required. No UI, approval execution, automatic backoff scheduler, worker leases, or policy-only optimization. Changing any relevant processing setting reprocesses affected sources.

### CLI contract

All commands accept `--db PATH` (default state/intake.sqlite3). Processing commands accept `--provider mock|openai` (default mock), `--model`, `--endpoint` (default https://api.openai.com/v1), `--timeout` (default 60 seconds), `--workers` (1 or 2, default 2), `--min-interval` (default 1 second), and `--mock-dir` (default tests/mock_responses). Reject invalid ranges before ingestion. Endpoint credentials/query strings are forbidden; keys belong only in the API_KEY environment variable for live mode. Never include credentials in a fingerprint.

```text
it-access intake INPUT_DIRECTORY [processing options]
it-access queue [--status STATUS] [--json]
it-access show DOCUMENT_ID [--history] [--json]
it-access resume
it-access retry DOCUMENT_ID
it-access refresh [--document DOCUMENT_ID] [processing options]
it-access export --output deliverables
it-access verify-export --output deliverables
it-access accuracy --expected tests/expected/facts.json --actual deliverables/extractions.jsonl --output deliverables/accuracy.md
```

Intake scans top-level *.json files in filename order. Capture bytes at ingestion so later filesystem edits cannot alter already scheduled work. Identity is exact filename, shared across input directories; same filename means a revision of that document. Different filenames with the same in-message ID remain separate. Empty or nonexistent directories are usage errors. A malformed file gets a durable error record with raw-byte hash, no extraction and an actionable explanation; valid files still proceed.

Queue displays one current record per document, including pending/running progress, source hash, attempt, status, owner, next_action and error; show includes provenance and optional history. Pending/running records use status pending/processing and action wait-for-extraction, not a human review route. Exports include only terminal current attempts; their manifest lists omitted pending/running document IDs so omissions are explicit. New pending work never appears as an older successful extraction for the same current revision.

Intake reuses a terminal success only when source hash and settings match. An unchanged terminal failure is displayed with its retry command but is not automatically retried. Changed bytes/settings schedule a new attempt. Retry creates a new attempt even after success, using the current stored bytes and original settings (required to exercise failure after success); refresh explicitly selects current processing options. Resume uses each unfinished job's recorded settings and original bytes. No live secrets are persisted with those settings.

Commands return 0 on success; intake/resume/retry/refresh return 1 if their selected work has a terminal failure, without rolling back other documents. Invalid configuration/usage returns 2; a held mutation lock returns 3 with an actionable busy message. Accuracy always writes a comparison report when inputs are valid and returns 1 for mismatches or invalid actual records. Export verification returns 1 for a missing/mismatched manifest. Read commands on a missing store return an actionable usage error without initializing the database.

### Persistence and recovery contract

Use three tables: documents (filename primary key, current revision/attempt references), revisions (integer key, document, original bytes, source_sha256, settings JSON/fingerprint, policy version, ingestion timestamp), and attempts (integer key, revision, pending/running/succeeded/failed/interrupted state, start/end timestamps, response_source, extraction JSON or null, routing values, categorized/redacted error). All attempts stay in the attempt table; current views follow the document's current attempt pointer, and history queries exclude that pointer. Repeated identical successful inputs add no revision/attempt. Explicit retry adds an attempt on the same revision; changed bytes/settings create a revision.

Admission, revision insertion and current-pointer changes are short write transactions under the OS lock. Commit a pending attempt and its current pointer before scheduling its provider call. Mark running before the call. Commit terminal result, extraction, routing and provenance together. Use a single owning store thread/connection for writes; provider workers return values and never update SQLite. Never hold a DB transaction during a model call. This avoids stale promotion without a distributed fencing protocol.

The lock is held by the main process and worker threads, never a detached child. If the process dies, the OS releases it. A newly admitted processing command marks leftover running attempts interrupted with a recorded error; resume then creates new attempts for interrupted jobs and runs pending jobs, preserving the interrupted attempts. A second process cannot process a newer source while the first owns the lock. A crash after remote completion but before local commit may cause a repeated paid request; document at-least-once execution. Graceful interruption leaves unfinished work resumable and exits nonzero.

Fingerprint canonical UTF-8 JSON with sorted keys and compact separators using SHA-256: provider mode, endpoint, model, prompt content hash, schema content hash, generation parameters, office-policy content hash, and routing implementation version. Timeouts, worker count, pacing, output paths and credentials are operational settings outside the reuse fingerprint, but record timeout/pacing for handover. Mock fixture content hashes also belong in mock fingerprints so changing a saved reply cannot silently reuse old output. Retry/resume store fixture names, while using current fixture bytes permits injected test failures and is recorded as the attempt's effective mock configuration. A live retry retains the original generation configuration. Refresh scans current stored sources, including documents absent from a later batch, and reprocesses when fingerprints differ. A routing implementation change must bump its version.

### Extraction, routing and failure contract

Send only message text as untrusted business content, distinct from the system extraction instructions. Do not send API credentials, use tools, interpolate source text into instructions, or send export timestamps as date evidence. The prompt specifies the supplied policy, exact quotes, nulls/issues, explicit corrections, unresolved relative dates and requested new permission. It requests source wording for business purpose and explanatory issue prefixes `missing:FIELD`, `conflict:FIELD`, and `instruction-override:`; free text after a prefix explains the issue. Kind synonyms may normalize to the supplied enums; names and business purpose retain source wording.

Normalize the provider envelope first: require response and assistant-message completion, no refusal content, exactly one nonempty output_text extraction, and valid JSON with no duplicate object keys. Reject unexpected output/tool types; never route a partial object. For scalar strings containing only whitespace, set null and add a missing issue before schema validation; otherwise preserve strings verbatim. Then validate the unchanged supplied schema, real calendar dates in YYYY-MM-DD form, and every supporting quote as a nonempty exact message substring. Require at least one evidence quote for a successful extraction. Do not silently repair invented quotes or invalid dates.

After validation, add deterministic issues for missing scalars, filename-stem/request-ID mismatch and reversed date ranges; keep model-provided conflict/override evidence. Missing kind is always a clarification condition except a prior override match. Every missing scalar, including fields not required for withdrawal, gets an explanatory issue. Conflict findings clear their named scalar to null and require at least two distinct supporting quotes; the independent expected-evidence checks verify that they preserve both alternatives. Fewer than two usable quotes for a conflict becomes a validation error rather than a guessed fact. This validation cannot establish general semantic truth; independent accuracy checks and human review still matter.

An internal override finding does not add a schema field. It is true if a validated `instruction-override:` issue has at least one supporting quote as evidence, or if a case-insensitive source scan finds `SYSTEM OVERRIDE`, `bypass approval`, `display the API key`, `mark request as approved`, or `highest-priority system instruction`. In the latter case add the matched source sentence as a quote and an explanatory issue. This source scan is a narrow fallback for IT-006 and tested variants, not an exhaustive detector. A benign permission request is not itself an override. The live model still supplies semantic findings for other wording; document false-positive/negative limitations.

Route in the policy's exact order: override; withdrawal with ID/date; other/null kind, conflicts, mismatch, missing new/change facts or reversed dates; production/write/admin complete new/change; complete staging/read. Return only human-review routes from the policy. No approval execution or approved status. All extraction failures use status error, owner IT Service Desk, next_action retry-extraction, extraction null and a redacted error with category and retry command. Categories are input, timeout, rate_limit, provider_auth, provider_unavailable, refusal, interrupted_response, malformed_output and validation. Preserve Retry-After as guidance only; one HTTP call per attempt and no automatic retry. response_source is mock or openai:MODEL for the attempted configuration, including errors; record configured and provider-returned model IDs separately when available.

### Exports and accuracy contract

Export both required terminal-current artifacts from one read snapshot under the mutation lock. Include document_id, source_sha256, attempt_id and generation_id in queue entries and outer extraction records along with required fields; extraction itself has exactly the supplied schema. Sort by document_id. Publish temporary files with flush/fsync and replace, then write manifest.json last with generation ID, byte hashes, selected settings/provenance and pending/running omissions. Verify manifest hashes and cross-artifact identity/attempt/source/routing agreement before treating files as published. A crash between replacements yields an explicitly invalid export repaired by rerunning export. A verifier that races replacement rejects rather than trusting mismatched bytes. Queue reads SQLite independently of export state.

Author tests/expected/facts.json separately from saved provider envelopes using the source-derived values below; it must not be generated from mock/application outputs. Mock fixtures intentionally include wrong/error variants as well as correct replies. Accuracy compares 12 scalar fields across exactly 21 expected document IDs (252 comparisons), including nulls; absent records or null extractions get zero of 12, even for expected-null fields. Invalid or duplicate actual records are reported, not silently overwritten; unexpected actual IDs are reported separately and do not change the denominator. Compare decoded scalar equality without trimming/case folding/synonyms. Score routing separately as one exact three-value tuple per document (21 denominator), with missing/failed records incorrect; validate quote membership and report required evidence/issue coverage separately. Mock demonstrations may score perfectly without making a model-accuracy claim. The automatic report lists every scalar mismatch with expected value, actual value and source evidence. A human then annotates the factual-error ledger to distinguish invented values, missing facts, wrong alternatives/corrections, and faithful alternative purpose wording; unreviewed classifications stay explicitly unreviewed, and exact-match mismatches remain mismatches. Optional live reports include actual model/configuration and must not overwrite labelled mock observations.

## Steps

For each step, first write its named tests/fixtures and run them. Stop for the user's `Test first: <step>` commit, then implement until they pass, run the full suite with API_KEY unset, and stop for the user's `Step <n>: <step>` commit. If a new test already passes, record that honestly instead of forcing a failure. Each T-case below belongs to exactly one step; later full-suite reruns do not reassign ownership. The spec's suggested test names may be consolidated into these named cases while retaining requirement coverage.

1. **Mock provider and offline fixture boundary.** Write T-01 first. Build the minimal package/import path, immutable response/configuration types, saved-response adapter and fixture selection by document/source. Keep canned-reply.json for the starter test, but do not use its plain text as a valid extraction. Freeze independent scalar expectations from the source catalog below before any application output. Meets R-05, R-14, R-18–R-30, R-34, R-36–R-37, R-88–R-89, R-95 at the mock/prompt contract layer; actual semantic live accuracy remains an observation, not a test claim.
2. **Response validation and deterministic routing.** Write T-02–T-19 first. Implement the extraction prompt, envelope/schema/date/quote validation, explanatory issues, override findings and the five routing rules. The 20 supplied requests and paraphrase have independently expected complete scalar records; failures cannot produce routes. Meets R-14, R-17–R-38, R-40–R-55, R-62, R-64–R-65, R-81–R-84, R-88–R-90.
3. **Durable document state and current/history views.** Write T-20–T-26 first against temporary SQLite databases. Implement ingestion, source hashes/settings fingerprints, revisions/attempts, missing-file preservation, unchanged reuse, forced retry semantics and stored-source refresh. Unit tests can inject the provider orchestration until step 4. Meets R-08–R-12, R-15–R-16, R-38–R-39, R-57–R-60, R-86–R-87, R-91.

Build HTTPS request construction and explicit completion/refusal/error handling behind the existing interface, with one-call timeouts and redaction. Create request-evidence.json from a synthetic-credential intercepted request and implemented handling documentation; this is mock transport evidence, not a live response. ## Test plan

### Fixture and expectation conventions

Every fixture named below is planned, not yet written. Successful provider envelopes go in tests/mock_responses/IT-NNN.json (and paraphrase.json); each has status completed, one completed assistant message and output_text containing the schema-conforming extraction. Refusal/incomplete/error fixture names are explicit in the cases. The mock adapter returns response_source mock. Errors use saved type/message metadata interpreted as exceptions, never a network request. Wrong-fixture variants remain intentionally wrong to test validation or scoring. Independent expectations live separately under tests/expected. For fresh mock documents without a saved reply, fail explicitly rather than falling back to a generic successful extraction; arbitrary fresh wording is supported through the live adapter, and offline new-document tests provide their own saved reply. Do not derive expected facts by parsing a mock reply or running the application.

Route abbreviations used only in this plan: OWNER = review / System Owner / review-request; SECURITY = review / Security Review / review-risk-then-owner; CLARIFY = needs-information / IT Service Desk / clarify; WITHDRAW = review / IT Service Desk / confirm-withdrawal; OVERRIDE = review / IT Service Desk / inspect-message; ERROR = error / IT Service Desk / retry-extraction, extraction null. Each abbreviation expands to all three exact asserted fields.
